svg.text: VISION v1 · BUILDING A BIGGER DATASET · D2

text.tspan: a quick automatic label, measured against the tracing
Instead of tracing from nothing: let a simple rule draft the mask, and let a person fix only what is wrong. How good is a draft made in a second?
A draft from colour alone, no tracing used

tspan.style: font-family:'DejaVu Sans Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:12.2px;font-weight:600;fill:var(--ink)

text.tspan: small gaps and removes specks. Then it is scored against the tracing, which it never saw.
A · The drafts, every mistake drawn

tspan.style: font-family:'DejaVu Sans Mono', Menlo, Consolas, 'Courier New', monospace;font-size:9.9px;font-weight:600;fill:var(--ink2)

text.tspan: The draft fails where colour fails: light clothes against a light wall are missed — the worst, person
found — and shadows and reflections on the floor are painted. Where clothes are dark and the wall is plain, it is close to the tracing.
the pixels a person would have to fix, against tracing from nothing

svg.text: every pixel the draft got wrong
every pixel the draft got wrong

text.tspan: Real labelling tools work this way: a draft — from a rule like this one, from a model trained earlier, or from a click on the object — and a person who corrects it with a brush or by moving corner points. The better the draft, the cheaper each label; the next pages make the draft from the model itself (
) and pick which photos are worth a
). Whatever draws the draft, a person still checks every label: a draft’s mistakes become the model’s.
